notes.meaning: God will draw His mighty sword to defeat Leviathan, the terrifying sea serpent. This monster represents cruel worldly empires and, behind them all, the devil himself. Even the most powerful and cunning enemies of God's people cannot escape His final judgment.

differ.view: Methodists traditionally see the three descriptions of the monster as pointing to three specific ancient empires: Assyria, Babylon, and Egypt.
Baptists have often identified Leviathan as antichristian world rulers like imperial and papal Rome, guided by Satan.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentators identify Leviathan as the devil defeated by Christ's death on the cross, or historically as tyrants like the kings of Egypt and Babylon.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that Leviathan draws on ancient Near Eastern imagery of a sea monster to symbolize chaos and rebellious spiritual powers opposed to God.

notes.meaning: God calls His people to sing a happy song about a fruitful vineyard. Earlier in Isaiah, God sang a sad song because His vineyard produced only wild, sour grapes. Now, through His mercy and discipline, His church is restored and brings Him great delight.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition reads this fruitful vineyard as a direct picture of the Church of Christ.

notes.meaning: The Lord Himself promises to watch over His vineyard every moment. He supplies it constantly with the refreshing water of His grace so it will never wither. He guards it day and night so that no enemy can break in and ruin it.

God explains that His anger against His beloved vineyard is completely gone. If harmful thorns and briers try to crowd the vines, He will march against them and burn them up like dry weeds. These thorny plants picture proud enemies who set themselves against God and His people.

differ.view: Baptists have often understood the thorns and briers as hypocrites and false teachers inside the visible church whom God will consume.

notes.meaning: Even those who were enemies are offered a gracious way to be saved. Instead of fighting God, they are urged to take hold of His protecting strength and ask for mercy. God repeats His offer of peace so that everyone knows how gladly He welcomes repentant sinners.

differ.view: Baptists emphasize that taking hold of God's strength means turning to Jesus Christ by faith, since Christ alone makes peace with God for sinners.

notes.meaning: In the days ahead, God's people will put down deep, sturdy roots like a healthy vine. They will sprout and blossom until their fruit spreads over the whole earth. This points forward to the spread of the gospel, which brings God's spiritual blessings to all nations.

differ.view: Some evangelicals expect a literal future regathering and earthly prosperity of national Israel during a millennium, while others see this fulfilled in the worldwide spread of the gospel through the church.

notes.meaning: The Lord asks whether He punished Israel as harshly as He struck down Israel's cruel captors. The clear answer is no. God disciplines His own children in mercy to correct them, but He destroys unrepentant persecutors in strict justice.

God measured out the trials He brought upon His people, taking care not to give them more than they could endure. Even when He sent them away into exile like a harsh desert wind, He kept the storm under His control. He handled them like a wise physician who only gives as much strong medicine as needed to bring healing.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition reads this as God judging the ancient synagogue with measured justice in proportion to its sins.

notes.meaning: The troubles Israel faced were meant to clean away their sin and draw them back to God. The true proof of their repentance would be the complete destruction of their false gods. They would smash their pagan altars to bits like soft chalk and tear down every idol pole so they would never be used again.

differ.view: Baptists emphasize that earthly sufferings do not make payment for sins, but act as tools that lead sinners to repentance and to the true atonement found only in Christ.

notes.meaning: A once-proud fortified city is left deserted and turned into an empty pasture where calves graze on the weeds. As the dried-up bushes wither, women gather the broken twigs to build cook fires. Because the people refused to understand God and willfully stayed in their sins, their Maker shows them no pity.

differ.view: Many evangelicals interpret the ruined city as a picture of the worldly system of human rebellion, while others see it as the historical city of Jerusalem left empty during the exile.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentators have understood this desolate city either as Jerusalem chastised for its unbelief or as pagan Babylon.

notes.meaning: When the time comes, the Lord will harvest His people from the Euphrates river in the north to the border of Egypt in the south. He beats out the grain with gentle care, separating what is precious from the useless chaff. God will search out His scattered children and gather every single one of them home.

A great trumpet blast will sound out like the horn that announced liberty in ancient Israel. Those who were lost and suffering in exile in Assyria and Egypt will hear the call and return. They will assemble on God's holy mountain in Jerusalem to worship the Lord with thankful hearts.

differ.view: Baptists often apply the sounding horn to the gospel message, which calls individuals who are spiritually lost and perishing to find life and worship Christ.
Some evangelicals believe this describes a physical gathering of the Jewish people to Jerusalem at the end of time, while others see it fulfilled in the worldwide church gathered by the gospel.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition views the great trumpet as the preaching of the Gospel calling the Jewish people into the Christian faith.
